claim: Axonal arbors control how signals from individual neurons are routed within the mammalian brain.
source: The structure of axonal arbors controls how signals from individual neurons are routed within the mammalian brain.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract about the role of axonal arbors.

claim: Very few long-range projection neurons have been reconstructed in their entirety.
source: However, the arbors of very few long-range projection neurons have been reconstructed in their entirety, as axons with diameters as small as 100 nm arborize in target regions dispersed over many millimeters of tissue.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: Axons have diameters as small as 100 nm.

evidence: This is a factual statement about axon dimensions.

claim: Axons arborize in target regions dispersed over many millimeters of tissue.

claim: The platform enables visualization and reconstruction of long-range axonal arbors.

claim: The platform relies on a high-speed two-photon microscope integrated with a tissue vibratome.

claim: The authors reconstructed axonal arbors of multiple neurons in the motor cortex across a single mouse brain.
source: We demonstrate the power of this approach by reconstructing the axonal arbors of multiple neurons in the motor cortex across a single mouse brain.
evidence: This is a statement of the experimental demonstration performed.

claim: Long-range connectivity dictates how information flows between brain regions.
source: A core goal of modern neuroscience is to map neural circuits across the entire brain, as long-range connectivity dictates how information flows between brain regions (Bohland et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Brain-wide inter-areal connectivity has been probed using bulk injections of anterograde and retrograde tracers.
source: Brain-wide inter-areal connectivity has been probed using bulk injections of anterograde and retrograde tracers (Gerfen and Sawchenko, 1984; Hunnicutt et al., 2014; Luppi et al., 1990; Markov et al., 2014; Oh et al., 2014; Veenman et al., 1992; Zingg et al., 2014) and functional imaging methods with millimeter-scale spatial resolution (van den Heuvel and Hulshoff Pol, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Functional imaging methods with millimeter-scale spatial resolution have been used to probe brain-wide inter-areal connectivity.
source: Brain-wide inter-areal connectivity has been probed using bulk injections of anterograde and retrograde tracers (Gerfen and Sawchenko, 1984; Hunnicutt et al., 2014; Luppi et al., 1990; Markov et al., 2014; Oh et al., 2014; Veenman et al., 1992; Zingg et al., 2014) and functional imaging methods with millimeter-scale spatial resolution (van den Heuvel and Hulshoff Pol, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Intermingled neurons within a brain region have heterogeneous projection patterns.
source: However, intermingled neurons within a brain region have heterogeneous projection patterns (Nassi and Callaway, 2009; Shepherd, 2013) and carry diverse messages in the behaving brain (Li et al., 2015; Movshon and Newsome, 1996; Sato and Svoboda, 2010; Turner and DeLong, 2000).

claim: Neurons carry diverse messages in the behaving brain.

claim: Projection maps based on bulk tracer injections are comprised of multiple functionally and structurally distinct groups of neurons.

claim: Reconstructions of single neurons provide vital information about how neural signals are organized and transmitted across the brain to target regions.
source: Reconstructions of single neurons therefore provide vital information about how neural signals are organized and transmitted across the brain to target regions.

claim: Single-neuron reconstructions are critical for defining the fundamental cell types in the brain.

claim: The nervous system has long been viewed as a collection of discrete cell types defined by their developmental origins, gene expression, morphology, and function.
source: The nervous system has long been viewed as a collection of discrete cell types defined by their developmental origins, gene expression, morphology, and function.

claim: Axonal structure has been particularly useful in classifying projection neurons.

claim: The reliability and throughput of axonal reconstruction have remained limited by the necessity to restrict labeling to one or a few neurons in a single brain.
source: However, the reliability and throughput of axonal reconstruction have remained limited by the necessity to restrict labeling to one or a few neurons in a single brain and to manually track individual segments between serial sections, which are often deformed and may be damaged by standard histological processing techniques.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of prior methods.

claim: Manual tracking of individual segments between serial sections limits reliability and throughput of axonal reconstruction.

claim: The system is comprised primarily of commercially-available hardware and custom control software.
source: The system is comprised primarily of commercially-available hardware and custom control software (freely available at github.com/TeravoxelTwoPhotonTomography) and operates as follows: (1) the entire volume of space addressable by the stage system is partitioned into overlapping 3D tiles, each corresponding to a single image stack (Figure 1b); (2) tiles intersecting the exposed surface of the sample are marked for imaging (Figure 1c); (3) an image stack corresponding to each marked tile is acquired; (4) the integrated vibratome removes a portion of the imaged volume; (5) the precise surface plane of the remaining tissue is determined; and (6) this sequence of events is automatically repeated until the entire tissue sample has been processed (Figure 1d).

claim: Using point correspondences from lipofuscin, the tiles were registered and resampled into a set of non-overlapping image volumes precisely tiling the full brain.
source: Using these point correspondences, the tiles were registered (Materials and methods; Figure 3) and resampled into a set of non-overlapping image volumes precisely tiling the full brain.
evidence: This describes the registration procedure, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The resampled volume was hierarchically downsampled to produce additional representations at progressively lower resolution.
source: The resampled volume was hierarchically downsampled to produce additional representations of the volume at progressively lower resolution.
evidence: This describes the data processing for visualization.

claim: This multiresolution volume enabled efficient navigation at different spatial scales.
source: This multiresolution volume enabled efficient navigation at different spatial scales and neuronal structures, which appeared continuous across tile boundaries (Video 1), could be traced for over long distances.
evidence: This is supported by Video 1.

claim: Neuronal structures appeared continuous across tile boundaries.
source: This multiresolution volume enabled efficient navigation at different spatial scales and neuronal structures, which appeared continuous across tile boundaries (Video 1), could be traced for over long distances.
evidence: This is supported by Video 1.

claim: Sparse labeling was achieved by expressing Cre recombinase with a highly diluted adeno-associated virus while simultaneously delivering a Cre-dependent high-titer reporter virus.
source: Sparse labeling was achieved by expressing Cre recombinase with a highly diluted adeno-associated virus while simultaneously delivering a Cre-dependent high-titer reporter virus coding for a fluorescent reporter (e.g. eGFP) (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the labeling strategy, supported by a citation.

claim: Using this labeling strategy, 10–50 motor cortical neurons could be routinely labeled with high intensity in each brain.
source: Using this labeling strategy, 10–50 motor cortical neurons could be routinely labeled with high intensity in each brain.
evidence: This is a measured outcome of the labeling strategy.

claim: Brightly-labeled neurons were likely infected with a single copy of the viral plasmid encoding Cre but with many copies of the reporter gene.
source: Brightly-labeled neurons were likely infected with a single copy of the viral plasmid encoding Cre but with many copies of the reporter gene, thereby driving high expression in few cells.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism of sparse labeling.

claim: High-intensity labeling was necessary for high-contrast imaging of thin fibers.
source: High-intensity labeling (e.g. with viral vectors encoding bright fluorescent proteins like eGFP or tdTomato) was necessary for high-contrast imaging of thin fibers.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for imaging.

claim: Fine, long-range axonal collaterals were easily detected and resolved using this labeling strategy.
source: Using this labeling strategy, fine, long-range axonal collaterals—such as those innervating the contralateral motor cortex—were easily detected and resolved.
evidence: This is an observation about the imaging quality.

claim: These fibers were clearly discernable even in a maximum intensity projection through a large volume of tissue (2.3 × 1.3 × 1.0 mm) corresponding to >200 individual 3D tiles.
source: These fibers were clearly discernable even in a maximum intensity projection through a large volume of tissue (2.3 × 1.3 × 1.0 mm) corresponding to >200 individual 3D tiles (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The high excitation power needed to image axons with high SNR was not found to have a detrimental effect on resolution due to fluorophore saturation.
source: The high excitation power needed to image axons with high SNR was not found to have a detrimental effect on the resolution of our imaging system due to fluorophore saturation, as has been suggested (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Zipfel et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: Axonal segments associated with brightly labeled somata remained well-labeled through white matter tracts, at branch points, and at their termini in distant structures.
source: Axonal segments associated with brightly labeled somata remained well-labeled through white matter tracts, at branch points, and at their termini in distant structures, indicating high labeling intensity throughout each arbor (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The z-scored median peak intensity of individual axons was consistently high compared to background (15.0 ± 2.9 median ± standard error of the mean; 5–95% range: 7.0–70.7).
source: In this sample, the z-scored median peak intensity of individual axons was consistently high compared to background (15.0 ± 2.9 median ± standard error of the mean; 5–95% range: 7.0–70.7; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of SNR, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Datasets could be stored using lossy H.264 compression while maintaining high image quality.
source: Further, we found that datasets could be stored using lossy H.264 compression while maintaining high image quality.
evidence: This is an observation about data compression.

claim: At a compression ratio of 25:1, the SNR of small axons was reduced by only 4.8%.
source: At a compression ratio of 25:1, the SNR of small axons was reduced by only 4.8% (compression ratio determined in n = 996 tiles; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of compression effects, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Even with sparse labeling, axonal segments of similar caliber but originating from different somata cross paths with separations smaller than the diffraction limit of light.
source: Even with sparse labeling, axonal segments of similar caliber but originating from different somata cross paths with separations smaller than the diffraction limit of light, introducing uncertainty in the assignment of axonal identity following crossover points.
evidence: This is an observation about a limitation of the approach.

claim: Axonal crossovers introduce uncertainty in the assignment of axonal identity following crossover points.
source: Even with sparse labeling, axonal segments of similar caliber but originating from different somata cross paths with separations smaller than the diffraction limit of light, introducing uncertainty in the assignment of axonal identity following crossover points.
evidence: This is an observation about a limitation of the approach.

claim: The inability to unambiguously follow single processes has precluded extensive reconstruction of fine axonal collaterals in datasets containing multiple labeled neurons in the same brain region.
source: In the past, the inability to unambiguously follow single processes has precluded extensive reconstruction of fine axonal collaterals in datasets containing multiple labeled neurons in the same brain region (Gong et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The error rate in manual and automatic reconstruction of axonal processes from light microscopy datasets depends strongly upon the density of neurites within a local volume.
source: Since the error rate in manual and automatic reconstruction of axonal processes from light microscopy datasets depends strongly upon the density of neurites within a local volume (Gala et al., 2014), we assessed the feasibility of complete axonal reconstruction in this dataset.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The high density of processes at the site of viral injection prevented unambiguous reconstruction of many processes in this area due to axonal crossovers.
source: The high density of processes at the site of viral injection - the region containing the highest density of labeled somata - prevented unambiguous reconstruction of many processes in this area due to axonal crossovers (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The long-distance axonal projections of these neurons and their fine collaterals in target regions could be accurately reconstructed to a high degree of completeness.
source: However, we found that the long-distance axonal projections of these neurons and their fine collaterals in target regions could be accurately reconstructed to a high degree of completeness (Figure 6a; Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6a and Video 2.

claim: This level of completeness was facilitated by the labeling sparsity, high resolution imaging, and lack of discontinuities in the dataset.
source: This level of completeness was facilitated by the labeling sparsity, high resolution imaging, and lack of discontinuities in the dataset.
evidence: This is an inference about factors contributing to reconstruction completeness.

claim: 3–12 mm of axon could be reconstructed per hour, depending on local density.
source: Furthermore, 3–12 mm of axon could be reconstructed per hour, depending on local density—a substantial increase in throughput over classical serial-section reconstruction methods, even when samples contained only a single labeled neuron (Wittner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a measured throughput metric, with a citation for comparison.

claim: This represents a substantial increase in throughput over classical serial-section reconstruction methods.
source: Furthermore, 3–12 mm of axon could be reconstructed per hour, depending on local density—a substantial increase in throughput over classical serial-section reconstruction methods, even when samples contained only a single labeled neuron (Wittner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior methods, supported by a citation.

claim: The reconstructed group of neurons included two intratelencephalic (IT) projection neurons in layer II/III, two IT neurons in layer V, and one corticothalamic projection neuron located in layer VI.
source: This group of reconstructed neurons included two intratelencephalic (IT) projection neurons in layer II/III, two IT neurons in layer V, and one corticothalamic projection neuron located in layer VI (Figure 6a; Videos 3–5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6a and Videos 3-5.

claim: These neurons possessed extensive axon collaterals with each cell targeting a surprisingly diverse set of brain areas.
source: These neurons possessed extensive axon collaterals with each cell targeting a surprisingly diverse set of brain areas (Table 2, Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 2 and Figure 6a.

claim: The total axon length of these five neurons exceeded 300 mm (range: 23.6–121.2 mm).
source: Together, the total axon length of these five neurons exceeded 300 mm (range: 23.6–121.2 mm) and innervated 28 distinct brain regions (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the reconstructions, shown in Table 2.

claim: These five neurons innervated 28 distinct brain regions.
source: Together, the total axon length of these five neurons exceeded 300 mm (range: 23.6–121.2 mm) and innervated 28 distinct brain regions (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the reconstructions, shown in Table 2.

claim: The arborization of one individual layer V neuron was found to cover nearly the entire extent of the brain in the coronal plane.
source: The arborization of one individual layer V neuron was found to cover nearly the entire extent of the brain in the coronal plane (Figure 6b) and approximately half of the brain along the rostrocaudal axis, underscoring the importance of whole-brain imaging for determining axonal projection patterns.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: One layer V neuron covered approximately half of the brain along the rostrocaudal axis.
source: The arborization of one individual layer V neuron was found to cover nearly the entire extent of the brain in the coronal plane (Figure 6b) and approximately half of the brain along the rostrocaudal axis, underscoring the importance of whole-brain imaging for determining axonal projection patterns.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: One layer V neuron included an extensive projection to the taenia tecta.
source: Interestingly, this neuron included an extensive projection to the taenia tecta (Figure 6b), a region that exhibits only very sparse axonal labeling in bulk anterograde tracing experiments from motor cortex (C. Gerfen, unpublished data; Allen Connectivity Atlas: connectivity.brain-map.org/projection/experiment/141603190), further highlighting the diversity in projection patterns of similar neurons within a single brain region.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6b and comparison with bulk tracing data.

claim: The taenia tecta exhibits only very sparse axonal labeling in bulk anterograde tracing experiments from motor cortex.
source: Interestingly, this neuron included an extensive projection to the taenia tecta (Figure 6b), a region that exhibits only very sparse axonal labeling in bulk anterograde tracing experiments from motor cortex (C. Gerfen, unpublished data; Allen Connectivity Atlas: connectivity.brain-map.org/projection/experiment/141603190), further highlighting the diversity in projection patterns of similar neurons within a single brain region.
evidence: This is supported by unpublished data and the Allen Connectivity Atlas.

claim: All four reconstructed IT neurons projected to the contralateral motor cortex.
source: For example, in this limited dataset, all four reconstructed IT neurons projected to the contralateral motor cortex.
evidence: This is an observation from the reconstructions.

claim: The contralateral cortical projections of the two layer V neurons spanned a similar distance along the anterior–posterior (A–P) axis (red: 2152 um; black: 2096 um).
source: The contralateral cortical projections of the two layer V neurons spanned a similar distance along the anterior–posterior (A–P) axis (red: 2152 um; black: 2096 um).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the reconstructions.

claim: The terminal fields of the two layer V neurons were offset along the A-P axis by an amount closely mirroring the A-P offset between their corresponding somata (distance between projection centroids = 490 µm, A-P distance between somata = 513 um).
source: However, their terminal fields were offset along this axis by an amount closely mirroring the A-P offset between their corresponding somata (Figure 7a,b; distance between projection centroids = 490 µm, A-P distance between somata = 513 um).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the reconstructions, supported by data shown in Figure 7a,b.

claim: This relationship suggests that these projections might target a continuum of cortical locations rather than a single discrete structure.
source: This relationship suggests that these projections might target a continuum of cortical locations rather than a single discrete structure.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed relationship.

claim: The contralateral cortical projection of both layer II neurons targeted a similar location along the A-P axis more posterior than both somata (distance between projection centroids = 32 µm; A-P distance between somata = 271 µm).
source: In contrast, the contralateral cortical projection of both layer II neurons targeted a similar location along the A-P axis more posterior than both somata (Figure 7c,d; distance between projection centroids = 32 µm; A-P distance between somata = 271 µm).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the reconstructions, supported by data shown in Figure 7c,d.

claim: Visualization of the complete axonal morphologies of individual neurons is critical for understanding how diverse neural signals are organized and communicated to distant targets throughout the brain.
source: Visualization of the complete axonal morphologies of individual neurons is critical for understanding how diverse neural signals are organized and communicated to distant targets throughout the brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of the work.

claim: The approach can be used to trace individual axonal fibers and fine axon collaterals across the brain to their termini.
source: We have developed an imaging system for whole-brain, high-resolution fluorescence imaging and demonstrate that this approach can be used to trace individual axonal fibers and fine axon collaterals across the brain to their termini (Video 2) and thereby map the long-distance projections of single neurons (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Video 2 and Figure 6.

claim: The approach can be used to map the long-distance projections of single neurons.
source: We have developed an imaging system for whole-brain, high-resolution fluorescence imaging and demonstrate that this approach can be used to trace individual axonal fibers and fine axon collaterals across the brain to their termini (Video 2) and thereby map the long-distance projections of single neurons (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Video 2 and Figure 6.

claim: Reconstruction of axonal processes with light microscopy requires 3D, diffraction-limited imaging and a high-NA optical system.
source: Reconstruction of axonal processes with light microscopy requires 3D, diffraction-limited imaging and a high-NA optical system in order to effectively identify and disambiguate axons originating from different cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for reconstruction.

claim: Light scattering within tissue must be minimized in order to image full 3D volumes.
source: At the same time, light scattering within tissue must be minimized in order to image full 3D volumes.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for imaging.

claim: The authors extended block-face STP tomography to high-speed 3D imaging.
source: To achieve high resolution with minimal scattering, we extended block-face STP tomography (Portera-Cailliau et al., 2005; Ragan et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 2003) to high-speed 3D imaging.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on STP tomography.

claim: STP tomography has been used to image bulk axonal projections across the mouse brain.
source: In previous studies, STP tomography has been used to image bulk axonal projections across the mouse brain (Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Previous STP tomography has been limited to the acquisition of sequences of 2D images spaced at large intervals.
source: However, this approach has been limited to the acquisition of sequences of 2D images spaced at large intervals; high-SNR imaging of complete, 3D volumes - a necessity for tracing continuous neurites - has not been previously achieved using this approach.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of prior STP tomography.

claim: High-SNR imaging of complete, 3D volumes has not been previously achieved using STP tomography.
source: However, this approach has been limited to the acquisition of sequences of 2D images spaced at large intervals; high-SNR imaging of complete, 3D volumes - a necessity for tracing continuous neurites - has not been previously achieved using this approach.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of prior STP tomography.

claim: Selective plane illumination microscopy (SPIM) lacks the necessary spatial resolution (< 0.5 µm) for resolving close appositions between thin axonal collaterals within large tissue volumes.
source: Selective plane illumination microscopy (SPIM) (Dodt et al., 2007; Huisken et al., 2004) requires reduced acquisition times, but lacks the necessary spatial resolution (< 0.5 µm) for resolving close appositions between thin axonal collaterals within large tissue volumes.
evidence: This is a comparison with an alternative technology, supported by citations.

claim: Knife-edge scanning microscopy requires resin embedding of tissue samples that can quench or attenuate the fluorescence of native fluorophores.
source: Knife-edge scanning microscopy ( Li et al., 2010; Mayerich et al., 2008) represents a potential alternative, but requires resin embedding of tissue samples that can quench or attenuate the fluorescence of native fluorophores and produces tears in large tissue volumes along the edges of 'ribbon' sections.
evidence: This is a comparison with an alternative technology, supported by citations.

claim: Knife-edge scanning microscopy produces tears in large tissue volumes along the edges of 'ribbon' sections.
source: Knife-edge scanning microscopy ( Li et al., 2010; Mayerich et al., 2008) represents a potential alternative, but requires resin embedding of tissue samples that can quench or attenuate the fluorescence of native fluorophores and produces tears in large tissue volumes along the edges of 'ribbon' sections.
evidence: This is a comparison with an alternative technology, supported by citations.

claim: Knife-edge scanning microscopy has been unable to identify the vast majority of fine axon collaterals innervating many target structures.
source: While some axonal segments have been traced using this approach, it has been unable to identify the vast majority of fine axon collaterals innervating many target structures (Gong et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Large-scale electron microscopy is not yet feasible for volumes larger than 1% of the mouse brain.
source: Large-scale electron microscopy (Kleinfeld et al., 2011) offers the potential for dense reconstruction of neurites and synapses, but is not yet feasible for volumes larger than 1% of the mouse brain—precluding the reconstruction of long-range axonal projections.
evidence: This is a comparison with an alternative technology, supported by a citation.

claim: Sparse neuronal labeling is a fundamental requirement for the reconstruction of axon collaterals using light microscopy.
source: Sparse neuronal labeling is a fundamental requirement for the reconstruction of axon collaterals using light microscopy.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for reconstruction.

claim: Ambiguity is introduced when axons originating from different somata are juxtaposed with separations less than the resolving limit of the optical system.
source: Ambiguity is introduced when axons originating from different somata are juxtaposed with separations less than the resolving limit of the optical system (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: This challenge can be mitigated by imaging with the highest available resolution and imposing a high degree of labeling sparsity—but cannot be eliminated entirely.
source: This challenge can be mitigated by imaging with the highest available resolution and imposing a high degree of labeling sparsity—but cannot be eliminated entirely.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of the approach.

claim: Excessive labeling density was largely limited to the site of virus injection in the example dataset.
source: In the example dataset presented here, excessive labeling density was largely limited to the site of virus injection and therefore only precluded the extensive reconstruction of local fibers.
evidence: This is an observation about the dataset.

claim: Biological questions focused on local collaterals will require alternative labeling strategies that achieve greater separation between labeled somata.
source: Biological questions focused on local collaterals will require alternative labeling strategies that achieve greater separation between labeled somata to mitigate this limitation.
evidence: This is a statement about future directions.

claim: Sparse stochastic genetic methods and retrograde labeling provide straightforward approaches for labeling well-separated somata.
source: Sparse stochastic genetic methods (Rotolo et al., 2008) and retrograde labeling (Mazarakis et al., 2001; Wickersham et al., 2007) provide straightforward approaches for labeling well-separated somata.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reconstructing multiple neurons within a single brain provides a particularly rich description of axonal organization.
source: Reconstructing multiple neurons within a single brain provides a particularly rich description of axonal organization.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the approach.

claim: The spatial overlap or segregation of collaterals of different neurons within a single target region can be directly assessed at the micron scale.
source: The spatial overlap - or, alternatively, segregation - of collaterals of different neurons within a single target region can be directly assessed at the micron scale.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the approach.

claim: Comparison of projections of multiple neurons within the same population provides a means to better understand if topological organization in source areas is preserved in downstream structures.
source: Comparison of projections of multiple neurons within the same population provides a means to better understand if topological organization in source areas is preserved in downstream structures.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the approach.

claim: The fine-scale spatial relationships between axon collaterals from different sources may indicate how disparate streams of information remain isolated or are integrated in target structures.
source: In addition, the fine-scale spatial relationships between axon collaterals from different sources may indicate how disparate streams of information remain isolated or are integrated in target structures.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential insights from the approach.

claim: Such comparisons are challenging or impossible in datasets in which single neurons are reconstructed in different samples.
source: Such comparisons are challenging or impossible in datasets in which single neurons are reconstructed in different samples.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of alternative approaches.

claim: Whole brain imaging requires significant time (8–10 days).
source: Currently whole brain imaging still requires significant time (8–10 days) and resources (many TB of storage space).
evidence: This is a statement about current limitations.

claim: Whole brain imaging requires many TB of storage space.
source: Currently whole brain imaging still requires significant time (8–10 days) and resources (many TB of storage space).
evidence: This is a statement about current limitations.

claim: Labeling techniques that take advantage of multiple, spectrally separable fluorescent proteins should permit labeling of hundreds or even thousands of neurons in each brain while maintaining sufficient sparsity for single neuron reconstruction.
source: Labeling techniques that take advantage of multiple, spectrally separable fluorescent proteins (Cai et al., 2013; Shaner et al., 2005) and the targeting of several populations with non-overlapping projections in a single brain should permit labeling of hundreds or even thousands of neurons in each brain while maintaining sufficient sparsity for single neuron reconstruction (Gala et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a prediction about future capabilities, supported by citations.

claim: The high degree of automation employed in the acquisition procedure provides the opportunity for further scalability by taking advantage of multiple imaging systems operating in parallel.
source: In addition, the high degree of automation employed in the acquisition procedure provides the opportunity for further scalability by taking advantage of multiple imaging systems operating in parallel.
evidence: This is a statement about future scalability.

claim: The time required for manual tracing is likely to be greatly reduced as a result of recent developments in automation of neuronal reconstruction.
source: Although the time required for manual tracing remains substantial, this constraint is likely to be greatly reduced as a result of recent developments in automation of neuronal reconstruction (Gala et al., 2014; Jain et al., 2010; Peng et al., 2014) and the high SNR of axon imaging achieved with our approach.
evidence: This is a prediction about future improvements, supported by citations.

claim: Recent advances in imaging techniques, genetic targeting methods, and 'big data' tools have facilitated multiple, comprehensive large-scale efforts attempting to map neural connectivity.
source: Recent advances in imaging techniques, genetic targeting methods, and 'big data' tools have facilitated multiple, comprehensive large-scale efforts attempting to map neural connectivity.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader context of the work.

claim: In model organisms, connectivity mapping projects have largely focused on mapping local connectivity using electron microscopy.
source: In model organisms, these projects have largely focused on mapping local connectivity using electron microscopy (Bock et al., 2011; Helmstaedter et al., 2013) and the bulk projections of neural populations using light microscopy (Mitra, 2014; Oh et al., 2014; Zingg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In model organisms, connectivity mapping projects have largely focused on mapping bulk projections of neural populations using light microscopy.
source: In model organisms, these projects have largely focused on mapping local connectivity using electron microscopy (Bock et al., 2011; Helmstaedter et al., 2013) and the bulk projections of neural populations using light microscopy (Mitra, 2014; Oh et al., 2014; Zingg et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

source: In humans, atlases of gross physical and functional connectivity have been constructed from diffusion-tensor imaging and resting-state functional MRI datasets (Mori et al., 2009; van den Heuvel and Hulshoff Pol, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Techniques for atlasing the brain-wide axonal collateralization of single mammalian neurons remain unavailable.
source: However, techniques for atlasing the brain-wide axonal collateralization of single mammalian neurons remain unavailable, even though single-cell reconstruction has long been the gold standard for establishing the structure of long-range projections.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in available tools.

claim: Single-cell reconstruction has long been the gold standard for establishing the structure of long-range projections.
source: However, techniques for atlasing the brain-wide axonal collateralization of single mammalian neurons remain unavailable, even though single-cell reconstruction has long been the gold standard for establishing the structure of long-range projections.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of single-cell reconstruction.

claim: The approach described represents a crucial step towards filling the gap in available tools for mapping neural connectivity.
source: The approach described here for the efficient reconstruction of single-cell axon collateral maps represents a crucial step towards filling this gap in the available tools for mapping neural connectivity, and will contribute to the ongoing renaissance in large-scale neuroanatomy.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the work.

claim: The approach will contribute to the ongoing renaissance in large-scale neuroanatomy.
source: The approach described here for the efficient reconstruction of single-cell axon collateral maps represents a crucial step towards filling this gap in the available tools for mapping neural connectivity, and will contribute to the ongoing renaissance in large-scale neuroanatomy.
